scoring_note: Editorial musical hypotheses, not calibrated listeners. Specialist lane is proposed/inactive until routing and catalog activation are separately approved. Roots, dub, lovers rock, dancehall and reggae-pop are distinct traditions.

songs.title: Three Little Birds
songs.rationale: A soft, public reassurance whose optimistic refrain asks for release rather than confrontation.

songs.title: Marcus Garvey
songs.rationale: A commanding historical and political invocation that keeps pressure alive inside a hypnotic roots groove.

songs.title: The Harder They Come
songs.rationale: Personal resilience becomes a public declaration, with bright momentum and hard-earned defiance.

songs.title: Pressure Drop
songs.rationale: A brisk soul-inflected communal groove, driven more by infectious immediacy than slow immersion.

songs.title: Israelites
songs.rationale: A deceptively light hit carries economic strain, rewarding listeners who hear the story under the bounce.

songs.title: Night Nurse
songs.rationale: Velvet intimacy and aching need sit at the opposite end of the genre from public protest.

songs.title: Money in My Pocket
songs.rationale: A gently buoyant, personal romance uses reggae rhythm without the pressure of a manifesto.

songs.title: Legalize It
songs.rationale: A direct political demand where defiance matters more than gentle background comfort.

songs.title: Guess Who's Coming to Dinner
songs.rationale: Dense atmosphere and a watchful threat make this a patient, ominous counterweight to sunny reggae.

songs.title: King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown
songs.rationale: Space, echo and subtraction become the narrative; a defining contrast to singer-led directness.

songs.title: Java
songs.rationale: Melodica-led instrumental meditation values space and slow development over lyrical command.

songs.title: Fisherman
songs.rationale: Haunting harmonies and spiritual imagery pull the listener inward through ritual repetition.

songs.title: Bam Bam
songs.rationale: Playful and assertive dancehall voice, immediate and crowd-minded rather than atmospheric.

songs.title: Zungguzungguguzungguzeng
songs.rationale: A chant-like deejay performance privileges swagger, rough immediacy and group response.

songs.title: You Don't Love Me (No, No, No)
songs.rationale: A polished but wounded vocal on a dancehall pulse, exposing hesitation behind the beat.

songs.title: Handsworth Revolution
songs.rationale: UK roots reggae politicizes a specific place and makes group resistance the main attraction.

songs.title: Get Busy
songs.rationale: A high-motion, instantly communal dancehall crossover with almost no patience for quiet reflection.

songs.title: Welcome to Jamrock
songs.rationale: A huge, urgent social observation pushes reggae's public stakes to the foreground.

pairings.phrase: Tell the room it'll be alright, or tell it what must change?
pairings.why: Marley brings an immediate communal reassurance; Burning Spear unfolds a more demanding political meditation.

pairings.phrase: Defy the world, or let the rhythm do the talking?
pairings.why: Jimmy Cliff makes resistance explicit; Toots keeps its social energy closer to buoyant musical release.

pairings.phrase: Hear the struggle outside, or the ache behind the bedroom door?
pairings.why: Desmond Dekker's social observation carries public strain; Gregory Isaacs opens a private, tender space.

pairings.phrase: Keep it between two hearts, or take the argument to the street?
pairings.why: Dennis Brown wraps vulnerability in a friendly groove; Peter Tosh states an unambiguous public demand.

pairings.phrase: A shadow at the gate, or the promise that it'll pass?
pairings.why: Black Uhuru invite suspicious, layered immersion; Bob Marley replies with bright collective comfort.

pairings.phrase: Let the echo tell the story, or let a singer come close?
pairings.why: Augustus Pablo's dub strips away foreground reassurance; Dennis Brown keeps the groove human and accessible.

pairings.phrase: Stay inside the trance, or send the whole dance floor moving?
pairings.why: The Congos ask for slow spiritual attention; Sean Paul puts the moment and the crowd first.

pairings.phrase: Own the mic with a wink, or make it a megaphone?
pairings.why: Sister Nancy makes playful confidence contagious; Peter Tosh converts that command into sharper public argument.

pairings.phrase: A dancehall dare, or a neighborhood drawing a line?
pairings.why: Yellowman rewards immediate deejay charisma; Steel Pulse push collective political accountability.

pairings.phrase: One wounded heart, or a whole country on the witness stand?
pairings.why: Dawn Penn keeps intimacy exposed; Damian Marley places vivid public stakes over forceful rhythm.

pairings.phrase: Pack the floor now, or leave room for the echoes?
pairings.why: Sean Paul delivers full-body immediate company; Augustus Pablo lets space and time become the point.

pairings.phrase: A groove that shakes off trouble, or one that refuses to look away?
pairings.why: Toots offers lighter communal buoyancy; Damian Marley puts a harder public diagnosis into the beat.
